analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties for paying women less than men for equal work and bans asking about salary history.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 25 with 46 Democratic and Independent cosponsors, the bill went to the Senate labor committee and no action has been taken on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tightens the federal equal-pay law, which already says employers can't pay women less than men for the same work, but which is hard to enforce in practice. It raises the penalty for violations, makes it easier for workers to bring group lawsuits, narrows the excuses an employer can give for paying a woman less, and blocks employers from asking job applicants how much they earned at previous jobs. It also requires large employers to report pay data by sex, race, and ethnicity to the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than male coworkers doing the same work, especially those without access to detailed wage information. The bill makes it cheaper for them to win compensation (attorney and expert fees are covered), protects anyone who talks about their wages or files a complaint from being fired or demoted, and stops a history of low pay from depressing every future job offer. Families who rely on two incomes, and employers who already pay fairly (who lose the unfair advantage held by discriminating competitors), also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women facing unequal pay for equal work

how_it_helps.text: Adds compensatory and, in some cases, punitive damages to what a worker can recover under the equal-pay law, which previously only allowed back pay, and allows courts to award attorney and expert fees [S2].
Allows pay-discrimination cases to proceed as class actions under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, so workers can sue as a group instead of one at a time [S2].

Limits the employer's defense to a 'bona fide factor other than sex' that is job-related, consistent with business necessity, and accounts for the entire pay gap, so 'market forces' alone no longer excuse a differential [S2].

Broadens the definition of 'same establishment' so workers at the same company in the same county can compare pay, and makes it unlawful to fire or discipline workers for discussing or disclosing their own wages [S2].

Prohibits employers from asking job applicants for their wage history or using it to set pay, breaking the chain by which past low pay follows a worker to every future job; violators face civil penalties of $5,000 per first offense and up to $10,000 in damages per affected person [S2].

Requires private employers with 100 or more employees to report pay, hiring, termination, and promotion data broken down by sex, race, and ethnicity, with aggregate figures published so regulators and the public can spot patterns [S2].
Authorizes grants for pay-negotiation skills training for women and girls, and requires the Labor Department to report on the gender pay gap starting in the teenage workforce [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay workers of different sexes different amounts for the same work would face higher legal exposure, larger awards, and new reporting costs. Businesses with 100 or more employees would bear the cost of compiling and filing detailed pay data. Some of these costs could ultimately be passed through in prices or hiring decisions, and small businesses are largely exempt, so the burden concentrates on large employers.

drawbacks.text: The burden of proof shifts in the worker's favor once a pay gap is shown: the employer must prove its pay factor is job-related, consistent with business necessity, and accounts for the entire differential, and loses even then if a worker shows a cheaper alternative practice existed. Employers argue this makes it hard to justify market-based or individually negotiated pay differences and will drive up litigation costs [S2].

Mandatory pay-data collection (roughly a dozen compensation bands by race, sex, ethnicity, and job category) adds a recurring compliance cost for every employer with 100 or more workers, and employer groups have historically opposed similar EEO-1 pay-data requirements [S2].

The bill lets workers recover punitive damages for 'malice or reckless indifference' on top of back pay and compensatory damages, raising the stakes — and therefore the settlement cost — for any employer facing a pay claim, even a contested one [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The enforcement tools address a real gap: the existing equal-pay law covers only back pay, which makes most individual claims uneconomical to litigate, and wage-history questions perpetuate past gaps. The main cost falls on large employers in the form of compliance and litigation exposure, and the strongest fair objection is that narrowed defenses and class-action availability could penalize legitimate pay differences such as negotiated skills premiums. The bill does exempt small enterprises from most requirements, which limits the compliance burden on the smallest businesses but also leaves a large share of workers outside its data-reporting reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and immediately referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote scheduled; the Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the bill in the Senate on March 25, 2025, with 45 Democratic colleagues and, per the sponsor list pattern, Independent support among its 46 cosponsors; no Republican cosponsors appear on the bill [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral is the last entry in the action history [S4].
Because the Congress has not adjourned, the bill technically remains alive in committee and could still advance, though no action has been taken since its March 2025 referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers currently protected by weak enforcement of the equal-pay law, plus committee leadership free of the political cost of a floor vote. Workers with pay-discrimination claims remain without a remedy under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing no new pay rules

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1115 and organized 46 cosponsors to support the equal-pay enforcement bill.

for.name: Senate Democrats and independents (45)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill, representing every Senate Democrat-caucus member needed to show support.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: The bill sits in their committee with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled since referral in March 2025.

against.name: Senate Republicans (53 members)
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill without the bipartisan or majority support needed to reach the floor in the current Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors are Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats and no Republican has signed on, consistent with the party-line pattern of prior versions of this bill in the Senate.

industries.industry: Large employers (100+ employees) in all sectors
industries.note: Would face mandatory pay-data reporting, narrowed defenses in pay-discrimination suits, and exposure to compensatory and punitive damages and class actions. Their interest in weaker enforcement runs against workers seeking equal pay, though compliant employers face mostly reporting cost.

industries.industry: Human resources and pay-data/HR compliance services
industries.note: The 100-employee reporting mandate and new compliance requirements create demand for pay-equity audits, data systems, and consulting to help employers analyze and document pay decisions.

Higher litigation exposure and class-action availability mean more pay-discrimination suits to defend; the bill's fee-shifting also funds the plaintiff side. More litigation either way, though the subject matter affects workers' pay rights directly.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has 46 cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, in a Republican-controlled Senate; it has received no committee action since its March 2025 referral. In the 117th Congress an identical bill passed the House but died in the Senate (widely reported). The realistic path here is that it stays in the HELP committee without a hearing or vote unless the chamber's control or priorities change.
